286.t: The Supreme Band under Pete Lacasse, Eddie Jackson managing
286.s: Russ joined the Supreme Band with Lacasse as leader and Eddie Jackson as manager, around 1925-26, later playing the Royal Garden on Gravier Street.
286.q: Curbeck. He's pretty sacrifice. We left here a year. Curbeck. He called him Curbeck.

286.t: Piron's strictly reading band and singing for rich white audiences
286.s: Members of the Piron band are recalled; it was the best reading band in the city, and Russ sang for wealthy white dancers.
286.q: No, sucephone. He was telling me to use the bass drum, which he didn't use in bass drum. And I was... He was a little boy in there. Mm-hm.

308.t: Joining Piron's band in 1928 after Robichaux
308.s: Playing for Robichaux, he impressed Cottrell's circle and replaced Paul Barbarin when Barbarin left.
308.q: And, uh, what made me get into the Piran band was the carnival day of 1928, I believe it was. I was playing at the New Orleans Country Club, it was an open house.

308.t: After Robichaux: Piron again and having no band of his own
308.s: He went back to Piron in 1928 and says he never led a band under his own name.
308.q: Yeah. That was during the time when, uh, when Paul Bobberin, we left P-Rong Band to go with a kid, uh, Sonny Allen. Uh-huh. I mean, with, uh, Sonny Allen and them and Walter P. Sean, that's where I went, P-Rong Band. All that was in 1928. And I worked in that band a good while.

253.t: Early idols: Jimmy Noone, Tio, Piron and Robichaux
253.s: Asked who influenced him on arrival, Hall names Jimmy Noone and Lorenzo Tio, and recalls Robichaux's New York trip and Piron.
253.ch: New Orleans bands and Buddy Petit tours
253.q: He had your own style, didn't he? No, no, he was mentioning about the guy that was playing, you know. What was the guy who was working at the, working with, what's the name of this, Piku? Piku. Yeah, it was another fellow who used to work with Robichaud. Charlie McCurtis? No, no. One of them,…

568.t: Playing for the cabaret acts and joining Armand Piron's eight-piece band
568.s: The casino's backers, white acts and the hurt feelings with Roy Palmer and Baby Dodds; he lists Piron's band lineup and later takes it over.
568.q: Eddie Grossell's Casino. Yeah. You can put that down if you want. And he had, his partner was Del Peter, and his manager was a German Jew, Mr. Hunts. Hunts was his name. And everything was run through transportation of the theaters and all the Spokin people that came in town to shows. Like every…

662.t: Piron's society orchestra and its pianists
662.s: She heard Piron's society band and met it at carnival balls and the country club. She names its pianists. Everyone she played with read music.
662.ch: Other pianists and the New Orleans scene
662.q: Yes, when I faced young, the orchestra, Pierron's orchestra was a society band here. They were very good, I heard them. And then after we organized a large band, we would meet them playing the different balls, because at that time we were playing the carnival balls. And Pierron's band and our band…

126.t: Piron and Robichaux bands in New Orleans
126.s: Early professional influences were Piron at Spanish Fort and Robichaux on Bourbon Street, bands of seven or eight pieces.
126.q: Well, I can remember the first people, uh, with whom I was in contact, was, uh, Piron, who played at the, uh, uh, out of Spanish Fort New Orleans. He, there's a, a supper club out there that he played at all the time, and he was one of the favorites in New Orleans. As well as Robichaux, who used to…

818.t: Photo of the Al Streeman band on the Jung Hotel roof
818.s: Coquille identifies players in a 1930s photo he took on the Jung Hotel roof garden, and they talk about the hotel's big ballrooms.
818.ch: Opening and photographs of New Orleans bands
818.q: Well, let's see. Some of these, I can't remember exactly when they were taken. Now, this one was taken probably, I would assume, probably during the 30s. And it's a photograph that I shot myself up on a Jung roof, which I think nowadays is what, the Grand Hotel? It was a brand of change later to…

45.t: Career sequence after Perez: Ridgley, La Vida, Piron
45.s: Williams recounts going from Perez to La Vida, Ridgley's band, back to La Vida, then Piron from 1932 to 1935.
45.ch: Ridgley, La Vida, Piron and the Minstrels
45.q: After you left Perez, who did you play with? After I left Manny Perez. You mean the orchestra when I was playing on the roof garden? Mm-hmm. I told you I went down to La Vida. You went to La Vida. And then? Got with Ridgely. You with... With Bebe Ridgely's Tuxedo. That band split up at the time.…

776.t: Piron's band and Fats Pichon on the boat
776.s: Piron's band summered on the boat; Fats Pichon started with Piron.
776.ch: Bandleaders and talent on the boats
776.q: That must have been good. He had a good band. Piron had a good band. He used to go over this summer. He played Louisiana in the winter time and he lived on the boat in the summer. He had a good band. That's where the piano player has been at the old absent house now. It started with Piron. That's…

846.t: Society bands, Storyville and the Negro dance bands
846.s: He covers Piron's polished band, Oliver, Kid Ory, young Armstrong, Storyville's closing and the Negro bands, whose members held day jobs.
846.ch: Society bands and white New Orleans attitudes
846.q: Well, I still think that today, in your audience, in spite of a very remarkable awakening within the past 10 years, which is due to the younger generation suddenly discovering jazz and accepting it, that in the old folks' mind, it still has nothing of value. It's probably degrading, and... It…

847.t: The Piron band at the roof garden
847.s: He recalls Piron's sweet, concert-style violin band of about twelve pieces on Gravier roof garden.
847.ch: Desvigne compared; Piron, Celestin and rivals
847.q: But for solo, sitting there with his arm, solo. Did you ever hear the P-Rone band? I heard the P-Rone band once or twice. They was playing on a roof garden here. Oh, up there on the Gravier about? Yeah, Gravier. That was his favorite spot. He had that spot sold up. And whenever it would be a dance…

288.t: Silver Leaf as Robichaux's second band; replacing Piron at teas
288.s: He says the Silver Leaf was second band to Robichaux and Charles's orchestra was Piron's second band, taking his place at teas.
288.ch: Maple Leaf, own orchestra and rivals
288.q: Just like Charles' orchestra was Pierrot's second band. I see. Because Pierrot, you see when he left and went to New York, I'm the one who took his place playing those, do you remember, I was standing at afternoon teas where nobody else played there with him but him. Pierrot was the only one who…

572.s: Allen and Bauduc sort out which bandleader was the left-handed fiddler.
572.ch: Johnny Bayersdorffer band and early drummers
572.q: Oh, you're sure it was Robichaud? Piron is the guy that, that wrote this, uh, which I could similarize. Yeah.

84.t: Piron's polished band for the better class
84.s: Piron's arrangements demanded note-for-note playing for society audiences, unlike the rougher dance-hall bands, with Handy's halls named.
84.ch: Reading bands and the jazz scene
84.q: And other of his music he was, wrote there to play strictly about his music. And he was playing out there at Transcenius and, uh, and, uh, he was playing for the better class of...

56.t: Starting at Lincoln Park in 1908 after Robichaux
56.s: Ory followed Robichaux at the pavilion in summer 1908 and declined his offer.
56.ch: Lincoln Park and the name Kid
56.q: Then after, and I'd taken all Robichaux away, called the Yacht Club and the Country Club, up and down St. Charles Trees, the gymnasium. Then he'd come and say, young man, you play a nice horn. He'd say, I'd like you to work with me. I said, thank you, Mr. Robichaux, I'm doing all right. Called him…

303.t: Johnny Long and Ray Anthony at the Blue Room
303.s: Programs show Johnny Long's band opening at the Blue Room, and Riddick shows another band with Billy Neuberger.
303.ch: Scrapbook: Blue Room acts and the United Fruit ship
303.q: All right. This is whose band? Is this Johnny Long? Mm-hmm. Johnny Long's band. This is the first band that were playing there when we first went there. All the guys in the band were just as fine a fellas as you ever met. And Long had his head so high in the air he never realized anyone was living.…
